statement: N fertilizer for the cash crop may need to rise after a high-residue cereal cover crop
applies_to: after cereal rye, wheat, oats at flowering
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Residue with C:N above 30:1 is expected to immobilize N early in decomposition
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Legumes can contribute 15 to 200 lb N/ac to the following crop, typical 50 to 100
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: C:N of mature legume residues varies from 25:1 to 9:1
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: C:N of pure rye ranged from 30:1 to 66:1 across several spring kill dates (Maryland studies)
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Hairy vetch C:N 8:1 to 15:1; rye C:N 25:1 to 55:1
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Brassica roots C:N 20-30, shoots 10-20; decomposition faster than winter rye; a winter-killed radish cover releases N early in spring
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Rye can take up and hold up to 100 lb N/ac until spring, 25 to 50 typical
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Late-summer oats can absorb as much as 77 lb N/ac in an eight to ten week period
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: On-farm report, south-central Kansas: Austrian winter peas gave 90 to 120 lb N/ac to the following grain sorghum; 25-30 lb N/ac were available as nitrate at incorporation
applies_to: Austrian winter pea after wheat (sandy loam, Partridge KS)
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)
note: single farm report in the SARE book, not a trial

statement: Spring cool-season cover crops before wheat produced about 3100 kg/ha biomass on average
source: Simon, L. M. (2024) Cover crops to regenerate soils and increase profitability in dryland crop production in the semi-arid central Great Plains, PhD dissertation, Kansas State University
note: read from the repository abstract page

statement: Warm-season cover crops after wheat produced about 3800 kg/ha biomass on average
source: Simon, L. M. (2024) Cover crops to regenerate soils and increase profitability in dryland crop production in the semi-arid central Great Plains, PhD dissertation, Kansas State University

statement: Profile plant-available water at wheat planting was about 21 mm greater with fallow than with cover crops
source: Simon, L. M. (2024) Cover crops to regenerate soils and increase profitability in dryland crop production in the semi-arid central Great Plains, PhD dissertation, Kansas State University

statement: Grain sorghum yields were 11 % less following standing or grazed cover crops than following fallow
applies_to: grain sorghum after cover crops that replaced fallow
source: Simon, L. M. (2024) Cover crops to regenerate soils and increase profitability in dryland crop production in the semi-arid central Great Plains, PhD dissertation, Kansas State University

statement: Average wheat yields were unaffected by fallow management or tillage (no percentage given in the abstract)
source: Simon, L. M. (2024) Cover crops to regenerate soils and increase profitability in dryland crop production in the semi-arid central Great Plains, PhD dissertation, Kansas State University

statement: Crop residue cover was 80 % with cover crops against 68 % with fallow
source: Simon, L. M. (2024) Cover crops to regenerate soils and increase profitability in dryland crop production in the semi-arid central Great Plains, PhD dissertation, Kansas State University

statement: Cover crops use soil water while growing; the time of termination becomes more critical as the probability of precipitation decreases
source: Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd ed., SARE Handbook Series Book 9 (3rd printing 2012)

statement: Non-irrigated cropland, zone 1: terminate cover crops 35 days or earlier before planting (late spring to fall seeded crops)
source: NRCS Cover Crop Termination Guidelines, Non-Irrigated Cropland, June 2013

statement: Non-irrigated cropland, zone 2: terminate cover crops 15 days or earlier before planting (late spring to fall seeded crops)
source: NRCS Cover Crop Termination Guidelines, Non-Irrigated Cropland, June 2013

statement: Cover crops in an irrigated cropping system are not restricted to a termination zone but terminated before the crop emerges
source: NRCS Cover Crop Termination Guidelines, Non-Irrigated Cropland, June 2013
